B. Copper sulphate, locally known as Neela Thotha, is widely available for agricultural use and traditional purposes, frequently used in self-poisoning.
C. Organophosphates are insecticides.
D. Sodium cyanide is a rapid cellular asphyxiant.
E. Aluminum phosphide is a fumigant producing lethal phosphine gas.

git-forensic.stem: What is the pathological appearance of the liver in advanced Wilson disease (cirrhosis)?
options: Nutmeg liver due to chronic passive congestion
Macronodular or micronodular cirrhosis with variable steatosis and copper accumulation
Primary hepatocellular carcinoma without underlying fibrosis
why: A. Nutmeg liver is seen in right-sided heart failure.
B. Chronic copper toxicity leads to progressive hepatic inflammation, necrosis, and macronodular or mixed cirrhosis.
C. Polycystic liver is a congenital anomaly.
D. Hydatid cysts are caused by Echinococcus granulosus tapeworm larvae.
E. Cirrhosis is almost invariably present before HCC develops in Wilson disease.

git-forensic.stem: Which chelating agent acts by forming a heterocyclic ring with copper and is administered orally as first-line maintenance therapy for Wilson disease?
why: A. Dimercaprol is an injectable oil-based chelator.
B. D-penicillamine is an orally active chelating agent that binds copper and promotes its urinary excretion, serving as a primary treatment for Wilson disease.
C. Deferoxamine chelates iron.
D. CaNa2EDTA chelates lead.
E. Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase.

git-forensic.stem: What is the typical finding on a 24-hour urinary copper excretion test in a symptomatic patient with Wilson disease?
why: A. Decreased urinary copper is not seen in active Wilson disease.
B. Urinary copper excretion is significantly elevated (> 100 micrograms/24 hours, often > 400 micrograms) due to high free serum copper spilling into the urine.
C. It is markedly elevated, not zero.
D. It remains persistently elevated in untreated symptomatic patients.
E. It is elevated regardless of pregnancy status.

git-forensic.stem: Which occupational hazard in ship-breaking yards in Pakistan (such as Gadani) is most directly associated with heavy metal poisoning among labourers cutting steel plates?
options: Lead paint fumes and lead-based anti-corrosive coatings
why: A. Mercury is not the primary coating on ship hulls.
B. Torch-cutting of steel plates coated with lead-based anti-corrosive paints generates toxic lead fumes and dust inhaled by workers.
C. Arsenic is not the main structural hazard.
D. Cadmium is less common than lead paint in ship structures.
E. Cyanide gas is not standard in ship plate coatings.

git-forensic.stem: What is the mechanism by which copper toxicity causes acute renal failure?
options: Direct tubular cytotoxicity and free haemoglobin-induced tubular obstruction following massive hemolysis
why: A. Immune complex deposition causes glomerulonephritis, not acute copper necrosis.
B. Ingested copper causes intravascular haemolysis releasing free haemoglobin, which together with direct copper tubular toxicity leads to acute tubular necrosis.
C. Infection is secondary, not the primary mechanism.
D. Renal artery thrombosis is caused by thromboembolism.
E. Copper does not precipitate as large ureteral crystals.

git-forensic.stem: Which clinical feature helps differentiate acute lead poisoning from acute abdomen of surgical origin (such as appendicitis)?
options: Presence of severe guarding and rebound tenderness
Colicky abdominal pain relieved by firm pressure, associated with constipation and absence of localized peritoneal signs
why: A. Surgical emergencies show guarding and rebound tenderness, which are absent in lead colic.
B. Lead colic presents with severe diffuse abdominal cramps that are paradoxically relieved by pressure, accompanied by absolute constipation and normal soft abdomen without peritonism.
C. High fever points to infection or inflammation, not lead colic.
D. Bloody diarrhoea points to dysentery or ischemic colitis.
E. Right lower quadrant mass points to appendiceal abscess or malignancy.

git-forensic.stem: What is the function of the ATP7B protein that is mutated in Wilson disease?
options: To absorb iron from the duodenal brush border
To transport copper into the trans-Golgi network for incorporation into ceruloplasmin and excretion into bile
To filter amino acids in the renal glomerulus
To regulate calcium influx into cardiac myocytes
To synthesize hemoglobin in developing erythroblasts
why: A. Iron absorption is mediated by divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) and ferroportin.
B. ATP7B is a copper-transporting P-type ATPase responsible for loading copper onto ceruloplasmin and excreting excess copper into bile.
C. Renal filtration is passive across the glomerular membrane.
D. Calcium influx is handled by L-type calcium channels.
E. Hemoglobin synthesis uses different enzymatic machinery.

git-forensic.stem: Which diagnostic imaging modality is most sensitive for detecting early lenticular nucleus degeneration in neurological Wilson disease?
options: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the brain
Computed Tomography (CT) scan of the head
why: A. Plain X-rays cannot visualize deep brain structures.
B. MRI brain is highly sensitive, demonstrating characteristic T2 hyperintensities and signal changes in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem (face of the giant panda sign).
C. CT scan is less sensitive than MRI for early subcortical changes.
D. EEG detects electrical seizure activity, not structural metal deposition.
E. Carotid Doppler evaluates extracranial vascular flow.

git-forensic.stem: What is the role of potassium ferrocyanide when used as an antidote in acute copper sulphate ingestion?
options: It acts as a central nervous system stimulant.
It reacts with copper to form insoluble copper ferrocyanide, preventing systemic absorption.
It chelates copper in the bloodstream.
It coats the entire intestinal tract to prevent bacterial infection.
why: A. It is not a CNS stimulant.
B. Potassium ferrocyanide (starch or wash) precipitates ingested copper into insoluble, non-toxic copper ferrocyanide, limiting GI absorption.
C. It does not alter urinary pH for diuresis.
D. Chelation occurs in blood via agents like penicillamine, whereas ferrocyanide acts directly in the stomach lumen.
E. It is a chemical precipitant, not a mechanical mucosal coating agent.

git-forensic.stem: Which symptom complex is characteristic of chronic copper toxicity in occupational settings (such as vineyard sprayers or copper miners)?
options: Metal fume fever, greenish discoloration of hair and skin, and mucosal irritation
Progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy with wrist drop
Severe bone resorption and osteomalacia (Itai-Itai disease)
Hyperpigmentation and Mee's lines on nails
why: A. Occupational copper exposure causes metal fume fever, greenish hair/skin discoloration, and upper airway irritation.
B. Wrist drop is classic for lead poisoning.
C. Itai-Itai disease is caused by cadmium toxicity.
D. Pulmonary fibrosis from mining dust is silicosis.
E. Mee's lines are seen in arsenic or thallium poisoning.

git-forensic.stem: What is the recommended dietary management for a patient diagnosed with Wilson disease?
options: High-copper diet including shellfish, nuts, chocolate, liver, and mushrooms
Avoidance of copper-rich foods such as shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate, and mushrooms
Strict vegetarian diet with unlimited legume consumption
High-iron diet with red meat restriction
Low-protein diet identical to hepatic encephalopathy protocols
why: A. High-copper foods would worsen hepatic copper overload.
B. Patients must avoid foods naturally high in copper, such as shellfish, liver, nuts, chocolate, and mushrooms, to reduce dietary copper load.
C. Legumes can contain moderate copper and are restricted.
D. Iron restriction is for hemochromatosis, not Wilson disease.
E. Protein restriction is only used during acute hepatic encephalopathy crises, not as baseline Wilson diet.

git-forensic.stem: Which legal document in Pakistan mandates medical examination and safety precautions for workers handling hazardous substances like lead?
options: Factories Act 1934 and Provincial Occupational Health and Safety Acts
why: A. PPC deals with criminal offences and punishments.
B. CrPC governs criminal court procedures.
C. The Factories Act and occupational safety laws regulate industrial working conditions, safety equipment, and medical surveillance.
D. Qanun-e-Shahadat governs the law of evidence in courts.
E. Medical commission acts regulate medical education and practice.

git-forensic.stem: What is the immediate cause of death in fulminant hepatic failure secondary to Wilson disease?
options: Massive cerebral oedema, intracranial hypertension, and multi-organ dysfunction syndrome
why: A. Fulminant hepatic failure causes severe cerebral oedema, brain herniation, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure leading to death.
B. Aortic aneurysm is unrelated to acute liver failure.
C. Myocardial infarction is a primary cardiac event.
D. Pneumothorax is a pleural cavity condition.
E. Pulmonary embolism arises from deep venous thrombosis.

git-forensic.stem: Which of the following food poisoning pathogens is classically associated with the ingestion of inadequately cooked home-canned vegetables causing cranial nerve palsies?
why: Clostridium perfringens causes late-onset diarrhoea.
Bacillus cereus is associated with fried rice.
Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin causes descending paralysis and cranial nerve signs.
Staphylococcus aureus causes rapid onset vomiting.
Vibrio cholerae causes rice-water stools.

git-forensic.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with projectile vomiting 3 hours after eating a cream-filled pastry at a wedding. Which mechanism is most likely responsible?
why: Staph aureus produces pre-formed enterotoxin in food.
Infection usually has a longer incubation.
Invasion is characteristic of Salmonella.
Toxin production in the gut is typical of C. Perfringens.
Allergic reactions do not typically present with this timeline.

git-forensic.stem: Which bacterium is the most common cause of food poisoning in Pakistan, often transmitted via contaminated water or raw poultry?
why: Salmonella is common but Campylobacter remains a leading cause.
Campylobacter jejuni is a primary cause of bacterial gastroenteritis.
Shigella is associated with dysentery.
E. Coli is diverse but less commonly isolated than Campylobacter in routine surveys.
Listeria is rare.

git-forensic.stem: A patient consumes leftover fried rice stored at room temperature. What is the specific toxin produced by the causative organism?
why: Cereulide is the emetic toxin of Bacillus cereus.
Botulinum is from Clostridium.
Enterotoxin A is from Staph aureus.
Alpha toxin is from C. Perfringens.
Shiga toxin is from Shigella.

git-forensic.stem: Which of the following food poisoning types is associated with a 'double-zoning' phenomenon on blood agar?
why: Staph aureus shows golden colonies.
Salmonella does not show double zones.
Clostridium perfringens produces alpha-toxin causing double zone of haemolysis.
Vibrio shows green colonies on TCBS.
Bacillus cereus shows beta-haemolysis.

git-forensic.stem: In the context of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), adulteration of food that causes death is punishable under which section?
why: Section 272/273 covers adulteration generally.
Section 302 covers Qatl-i-Amd (intentional murder).
Section 320 covers death by rash/negligent driving.
Section 337 relates to hurt.
If death is caused by knowing the food is poisonous, it falls under homicide provisions.

git-forensic.stem: Which fish is specifically noted for causing Scombroid poisoning when improperly stored?
why: Tuna (scombroid fish) when decomposed produces histamine.
Pomfret is a common edible fish.
Rohu is a freshwater fish.
Catfish is freshwater.
Shark is not typical for Scombroid.

git-forensic.stem: A patient experiences numbness around the mouth and tingling in extremities shortly after eating a pufferfish. What is the toxin involved?
why: Tetrodotoxin is found in pufferfish (Fugu).
Saxitoxin is from shellfish.
Ciguatoxin is from reef fish.
Muscarine is from mushrooms.
Aflatoxin is a fungal toxin.

git-forensic.stem: What is the primary management for a patient with suspected Staphylococcal food poisoning?
why: Antibiotics are ineffective as it is a toxin-mediated illness.
Antivirals have no role.
Supportive hydration is the mainstay of treatment.
Antitoxin is not indicated.
Lavage is unnecessary for toxin ingestion.

git-forensic.stem: Which of the following is a heat-stable enterotoxin produced by Staphylococcus aureus?
why: Enterotoxin A is heat-stable and causes gastroenteritis.
Beta toxin is a sphingomyelinase.
Exfoliative toxin causes scalded skin syndrome.
TSST-1 causes toxic shock.
Alpha haemolysin causes cell lysis.

git-forensic.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with severe vomiting, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea 3 hours after consuming a custard-filled pastry. What is the most likely bacterial toxin responsible?
why: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin causes rapid onset (1-6 hours) food poisoning due to heat-stable toxin.
Bacillus cereus (emetic type) has a similar onset but is associated with fried rice.
Clostridium botulinum presents with neurological signs, not just GI.
Salmonella has a longer incubation period (12-72 hours).
Vibrio parahaemolyticus is associated with seafood and longer incubation.

git-forensic.stem: Which of the following food poisoning agents is associated with the 'fried rice syndrome' and has both an emetic and a diarrhoeal form?
why: Bacillus cereus is classic for fried rice syndrome; emetic form (cereulide) and diarrhoeal form (enterotoxin).
Clostridium perfringens is associated with meat stews.
Shigella causes bacillary dysentery.
Campylobacter is associated with poultry.
Escherichia coli is associated with contaminated water.

git-forensic.stem: An outbreak of food poisoning occurs at a wedding after guests consume improperly canned meat. Patients develop descending paralysis and diplopia. Which toxin is involved?
why: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release, causing descending flaccid paralysis.
Tetrodotoxin is found in pufferfish.
Saxitoxin causes paralytic shellfish poisoning.
Aflatoxin is hepatotoxic/carcinogenic.
Ergot causes convulsive or gangrenous ergotism.

git-forensic.stem: In the medico-legal investigation of a suspected food poisoning death, which of the following is the most important site for the collection of viscera for toxicological analysis?
why: Stomach contents are the primary site for identifying ingested food-borne toxins or pathogens.
Liver is for metals and drug metabolism.
Brain is for alcohol and volatile poisons.
Kidney is for heavy metals.
Lung is for inhalational toxins.

git-forensic.stem: Which of the following is an example of an 'alkaloid food poisoning' where the grain is contaminated by a fungus?
why: Ergotism is caused by Claviceps purpurea infecting rye or wheat.
Lathyrism is due to Lathyrus sativus consumption.
Favism is an enzyme deficiency response.
Aflatoxicosis is fungal, but from Aspergillus.
Scombroid is histamine toxicity.

git-forensic.stem: A patient presents with 'peppery' taste in the mouth, flushing, and tachycardia immediately after eating spoiled tuna. What is the diagnosis?
why: Scombroid poisoning occurs due to high levels of histamine in spoiled dark-meat fish.
Ciguatera involves temperature reversal sensation.
Paralytic shellfish poisoning involves neurotoxins.
Mushroom poisoning presents with liver failure or muscarinic symptoms.
Heavy metal poisoning is usually chronic or non-seafood related.

git-forensic.stem: Lathyrism, characterized by spastic paraplegia of the lower limbs, is caused by the excessive consumption of:
why: Lathyrism is caused by the neurotoxin ODAP found in Lathyrus sativus (chickling vetch).
Millet is not associated with lathyrism.
Rye is associated with ergotism.
