blood-community.stem: What is the primary reservoir of the Dengue virus during inter-epidemic periods?

Birds are not involved.

locomotor-forensic.stem: When applying Miles' method of age estimation to adult skulls, the forensic odontologist assesses tooth wear. What is the fundamental principle underlying this method?

Too late.

locomotor-forensic.stem: Which of these variables is used in the 'Lamendin method'?
why: Too simple.
Lamendin's method uses height of dentinal transparency and periodontosis height relative to root height.
Not enough.
Not the primary variables.
Not the main variables.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: Which type of X-ray is most useful for seeing the entire dental arch in a single view for identification?
why: Only shows a few teeth.
Only shows crowns/proximal surfaces.
Only shows specific quadrants/arches.
OPG provides a panoramic view of the whole dentition.
Shows the skull, not clear detail of all teeth.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: The presence of a 'canine' in the lower jaw usually signifies an age of at least:
why: Too young.
Too young.
Permanent mandibular canines usually erupt around 9–10 years.
Too old.
Too old.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: What is the primary forensic use of teeth in unidentified remains?
why: Teeth do not indicate COD.
Identification and aging are the two pillars of forensic odontology.
Post-mortem interval is not determined by teeth.
MOD is not determined by teeth.
Dietary analysis is an academic, not forensic, primary use.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: What is the status of dental development in a newborn infant?
options: No teeth are visible in the mouth, but primary crowns are calcified
Teeth start to form after birth
why: Only primary teeth are present.
Permanent molars are deep in the bone.
Primary teeth have begun calcification in utero but have not erupted.
Permanent teeth are not fully calcified.
Formation starts in utero.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: The 'Bite Mark' analysis is primarily a tool for:
options: Determining the sex of the victim
Calculating the IQ of a suspect
why: Bite marks don't give age.
Bite marks are compared to dental impressions to link a suspect to a crime.
Not used for sexing.
Irrelevant.
Not for PMI.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of dental age estimation?
options: Teeth are durable and survive decomposition
It is unaffected by systemic diseases
It is highly accurate in all populations regardless of genetics
It requires standard reference populations which may not match the case
It is impossible to perform in living individuals
why: Durability is an advantage.
Can be affected by systemic issues.
Population variation is a known challenge.
Reference data from one population (e.g., Caucasian) may not be accurate for another (e.g., South Asian/Pakistani).
It is possible in living persons.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: Which of these factors is most likely to cause confusion in dental age estimation in a 30-year-old?
why: Hygiene affects wear.
Missing teeth change the arch.
Treatment alters root position and morphology.
Smoking causes staining and can affect periodontium.
All can complicate the forensic assessment.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: A forensic expert is examining the mandible of an unidentified body. Which of the following teeth is most likely to show the earliest complete root formation?
why: A: Maxillary central incisor roots typically complete at 10 years.
B: Mandibular first permanent molar is the first permanent tooth to erupt (age 6) and its root formation completes earliest among permanent teeth (approx. 9-10 years).
C: Mandibular canine root completion occurs later, around 12-13 years.
D: Maxillary second premolar root completion occurs around 12-14 years.
E: Mandibular second permanent molar root completion occurs around 14-16 years.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: A 35-year-old skeleton is found. Using Gustafson’s criteria for age estimation, which histological change is most indicative of the aging process in the tooth?
why: A: Enamel hypoplasia is a developmental defect, not an aging change.
B: Secondary dentine continues to form throughout life, reducing the size of the pulp chamber; this is a primary component of Gustafson’s criteria.
C: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a genetic developmental disorder.
D: Taurodontism is a morphological variation (enlarged pulp chamber), not an age-related change.
E: Supernumerary teeth are developmental anomalies.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: Which of the following is the most reliable parameter for determining age in a 10-year-old child using dental development?
why: A: Second molars typically erupt around age 12, making them a key marker for this age group.
B: Third molars usually start calcifying later (12-16 years).
C: First molars erupt by age 6-7.
D: Canines complete their crowns earlier.
E: Most deciduous roots have resorbed by age 10.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: According to the Gustafson's method of age estimation, which histological change is evaluated first?
why: A: Secondary dentine is the second parameter.
B: Attrition is the first feature listed in Gustafson's original 6-point criteria.
C: Periodontosis is the fifth parameter.
D: Cementum apposition is the fourth parameter.
E: Root transparency is the sixth and final parameter.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: In forensic age estimation, which tooth is most commonly used for radiographical assessment in children?
why: A: Not the standard for general age.
B: Mandibular molars provide the most consistent developmental data in childhood.
C: Canines vary widely.
D: Premolars appear later.
E: Third molars are for adolescents and young adults.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: What is the primary indicator of age after 25 years using dental examination?
why: A: Eruption is complete.
B: Root transparency (sclerosis) is the most accurate indicator after 25 years.
C: Pulp chamber decreases but is less reliable.
D: Enamel does not change significantly.
E: Variable and influenced by hygiene.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: Which of the following is considered the gold standard for dental age estimation in sub-adults?
why: A: Demirjian's is universally accepted for radiographic dental development in children.
B: Lamendin is for adults (root factors).
C: Gustafson is for adults.
D: Johanson is a modification of Gustafson.
E: Miles is for archaeological populations.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: A 16-year-old victim's body is found. Which radiograph is most critical for confirming their age?
why: A: Insufficient scope.
B: Limited view.
C: OPG captures all tooth germs and developmental stages needed for estimation.
D: Only shows crowns.
E: Used for orthodontics, not age.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: When assessing the age of an adult via teeth, which feature refers to the decrease in size of the pulp cavity?
why: A: Secondary dentine deposition gradually obliterates the pulp space over time.
B: Tertiary dentine is a response to injury.
C: Developmental defect.
D: Pathological or physiological process.
E: Occurs in childhood.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: The 'Nolla's method' of age estimation is based on what?
why: A: Gustafson's method.
B: Not a standard method.
C: Nolla's method utilizes 10 developmental stages from crypt formation to apical closure.
D: Cementum annulation is a separate technique.
E: Periodontal factors are separate.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: Which factor makes dental age estimation more accurate than skeletal estimation in children?
options: Less variation due to systemic diseases
why: A: Nutrition affects both.
B: Not true.
C: Dental development is genetically tightly controlled and less influenced by external factors like disease.
D: False.
E: Skeletal maturity is more sensitive to hormones.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

locomotor-forensic.stem: In Lamendin’s method, which teeth are most commonly used for age estimation?
why: A: Multi-rooted.
B: Developmental variable.
C: Lamendin’s technique specifically uses single-rooted teeth for measuring transparency and resorption.
D: For children.
E: Used, but not exclusive.
locomotor-forensic.topic: Personal identity II – age, sex, intersex and dactylography

resp-forensic.stem: A 25-year-old male is brought to the JPMC emergency department with severe, painful tetanic spasms, risus sardonicus, and fully conscious awareness of his surroundings. His friend reports he ingested a bitter powder found in a local market. Which poison is most characteristic of this clinical presentation?
why: A. Opium causes central nervous system depression, pin-point pupils, and respiratory depression, not tetanic spasms.
B. Strychnine is a classic spinal poison that blocks glycine receptors on motor neurones, causing uncoordinated, painful extensor spasms and risus sardonicus while consciousness remains intact.
C. Datura stramonium causes anticholinergic delirium, dry skin, tachycardia, and mydriasis.
D. Organophosphates cause cholinergic excess with SLUDGE symptoms and fasciculations, but not classical severe extensor spasms of spinal origin.
E. Cyanide causes rapid cellular hypoxia, bitter almond breath, and cardiovascular collapse.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following pharmacological mechanisms best describes the primary toxic action of Strychnos nux-vomica alkaloids on the central nervous system?
options: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
Competitive antagonism of glycine at postsynaptic inhibitory sites in the spinal cord
Agonism at gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptors
Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels on peripheral nerve axons
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondrial membranes
why: A. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of organophosphates and carbamates.
B. Strychnine acts as a selective competitive antagonist of glycine, the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord, leading to unopposed reflex hyperexcitability.
C. GABA-A agonism would cause central depression, whereas strychnine causes extreme excitation.
D. Voltage-gated sodium channel blockade is seen in local anaesthetics and tetrodotoxin.
E. Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation is typical of agents like dinitrophenol.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the botanical source of strychnine, a potent spinal poison frequently encountered in forensic autopsy cases across South Asia?
why: A. Papaver somniferum is the opium poppy, the source of opiate alkaloids.
B. Atropa belladonna is deadly nightshade, a source of atropine and scopolamine.
C. Strychnos nux-vomica tree seeds are the primary natural source of strychnine and brucine.
D. Cannabis sativa yields cannabinoids.
E. Erythroxylum coca yields cocaine.

resp-forensic.stem: During a medico-legal autopsy at Civil Hospital Karachi, you examine the stomach of a suspected strychnine poisoning case. Which macroscopic feature of the poison source is most helpful to identify in the gastric contents?
options: Small, flat, disk-shaped, silky grey seeds with radiating hairs
Dark green tubular leaves with spines
why: A. Silvery white metallic globules are characteristic of elemental mercury.
B. Nux-vomica seeds are characteristically disk-shaped, button-like, covered with fine silky grey hairs radiating from the centre, and extremely bitter.
C. Resinous lumps correspond to crude opium or cannabis preparations.
D. Bright yellow powder is typical of arsenic sulphide or certain rodenticides.
E. Spiny tubular leaves do not match nux-vomica seeds.

resp-forensic.stem: Which secondary alkaloid, structurally similar to strychnine, is co-extracted from the seeds of Strychnos nux-vomica and possesses similar but weaker convulsant properties?
why: A. Brucine is dimethoxystrychnine, found alongside strychnine in nux-vomica seeds, and acts as a weaker spinal convulsant.
B. Morphine is an isoquinoline/phenanthrene alkaloid from opium.
C. Atropine is a tropane alkaloid from solanaceous plants.
D. Nicotine is a pyridine alkaloid from tobacco.
E. Cocaine is a tropane alkaloid from coca leaves.

resp-forensic.stem: A patient poisoned with strychnine exhibits severe opisthotonos. Which muscle groups are predominantly responsible for this characteristic posture?
options: Extensors of the back and neck
why: A. Abdominal flexors would cause emprosthotonos, not opisthotonos.
B. Extensors of the back and neck are much stronger than flexors, leading to the characteristic backward arching of the body known as opisthotonos during a strychnine spasm.
C. Intercostal spasm causes asphyxia due to fixation of the chest wall.
D. Extraocular muscle spasms cause fixed gaze or trismus, not opisthotonos.
E. Plantar flexors are involved in general rigidity, but opisthotonos specifically refers to spinal extension.

resp-forensic.stem: Why does a conscious victim of strychnine poisoning experience exquisite agony during every convulsive spasm?
options: Because the poison destroys peripheral sensory nerve endings directly
Because all sensory stimuli provoke massive, uncoordinated reflex motor discharge without central depression
Because strychnine causes severe local corrosion of the gastrointestinal mucosa
Because cerebral ischemia leads to severe cortical pain perception
Because profound hypoxia damages skeletal muscle fibres
why: A. Strychnine does not destroy peripheral sensory nerve endings.
B. Loss of spinal inhibition means even a slight draft of air, light, or noise triggers a maximal, painful contraction of all skeletal muscles while consciousness remains fully alert.
C. Gastrointestinal corrosion is caused by strong acids or alkalis, not strychnine.
D. Cortical pain perception is intact because consciousness is preserved, but the agony arises from simultaneous titanic contraction of all muscle groups.
E. Hypoxia is a late complication, whereas pain begins immediately with the reflex spasms.

resp-forensic.stem: In the management of acute strychnine poisoning, which immediate supportive measure takes absolute priority to prevent fatal asphyxia?
options: Administration of strong central nervous system stimulants
Placing the patient in a quiet, dark room to minimise sensory triggers
why: A. CNS stimulants would worsen the convulsions and precipitate fatal spasm.
B. Sensory stimuli (noise, light, touch) trigger lethal extensor spasms; keeping the environment absolutely quiet and dark is crucial until anticonvulsants take effect.
C. Forced diuresis is ineffective because strychnine is rapidly metabolised and redistributed.
D. Atropine is the antidote for organophosphates, not strychnine.
E. Gastric lavage without prior sedation or airway control can trigger a fatal convulsive spasm.

resp-forensic.stem: Which pharmaceutical class of drugs is considered the mainstay for controlling acute muscular spasms and preventing respiratory arrest in strychnine toxicity?
why: A. Benzodiazepines and barbiturates enhance GABA-mediated inhibition, counteracting the glycine receptor blockade caused by strychnine.
B. Beta-blockers only control sympathetic overactivity and do not stop spinal spasms.
C. Opioids depress respiration and offer inadequate control of spinal motor hyperactivity.
D. Loop diuretics have no role in acute spasm control.
E. Calcium channel blockers do not reverse the central spinal hyperexcitability of strychnine.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the classic medico-legal differential diagnosis that must be carefully considered when evaluating a patient presenting with trismus, risus sardonicus, and tetanic spasms?
why: A. Tetanus (caused by Clostridium tetani toxin) presents with very similar trismus, risus sardonicus, and spasms, but has a slower onset and history of a wound.
B. Botulism causes descending flaccid paralysis, not spasticity.
C. Organophosphates cause cholinergic crisis and fasciculations, not fixed tetanic opisthotonos.
D. Arsenic causes severe gastroenteritis and peripheral neuropathy.
E. Diabetic ketoacidosis presents with Kussmaul breathing and dehydration.

resp-forensic.stem: Which chemical colour test is traditionally employed in the forensic toxicology laboratory to detect strychnine by producing a play of colours (deep purple fading to red and yellow) upon oxidation?
why: A. Mandelin's test (ammonium vanadate in concentrated sulfuric acid) produces a characteristic purple colour with strychnine, changing to red and yellow.
B. Marquis test is used primarily for opiates and amphetamines.
C. Liebermann's test is used for steroids and certain phenolic compounds.
D. Vitali's test is used for tropane alkaloids (atropine, scopolamine).
E. Copper reduction tests are used for reducing sugars.

resp-forensic.stem: In Pakistan, under the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), administering a noxious substance like strychnine with intent to cause harm or commit murder falls under which legal category?
options: Administration of poison with intent to hurt or kill
why: A. Hurt by dangerous weapons applies to physical weapon injuries.
B. Sections dealing with administering poison (such as PPC Section 328 or related hurt/qatl sections) specifically cover the criminal administration of noxious substances to cause harm or death.
C. Criminal negligence relates to failure in a duty of care, not intentional poisoning.
D. Accidental poisoning does not carry criminal intent.
E. Affray involves public fighting between two or more persons.

resp-forensic.stem: Post-mortem rigidity (rigor mortis) in cases of fatal strychnine poisoning exhibits a distinctive peculiarity compared to ordinary deaths. What is this classic medico-legal feature?
options: Rigor mortis is entirely absent due to exhaustion of muscle enzymes
Rigor mortis sets in with extreme rapidity (cadaveric spasm) owing to high muscular activity immediately before death
Rigor mortis is delayed for up to 72 hours
Rigor mortis affects only the lower limbs
Rigor mortis relaxes spontaneously within one hour of death
why: A. Rigor is not absent; rather, it is accelerated.
B. The extreme muscular exertion and terminal convulsions of strychnine deplete ATP rapidly, causing rigor mortis to set in almost immediately after death (often resembling cadaveric spasm).
C. Delayed rigor is seen in debilitating chronic diseases.
D. Rigor affects the entire muscular system.
E. Rigor does not spontaneously relax in an hour; it follows the normal post-mortem timeline after early onset.

resp-forensic.stem: Which post-mortem finding is most commonly observed in the lungs and heart of a victim who died during a violent strychnine-induced convulsive crisis?
options: Pulmonary oedema, petechial haemorrhages, and venous engorgement
Severe pulmonary fibrosis and pleural plaques
Myocardial infarction of the right ventricle
Fatty degeneration of the coronary arteries
Caseous necrosis of the hilar lymph nodes
why: A. Death from strychnine is typically asphyxial due to tetanic fixation of respiratory muscles, resulting in petechiae, cyanosis, pulmonary oedema, and dark fluid blood.
B. Pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic occupational disease, not an acute poisoning sign.
C. Right ventricular infarction is an ischaemic cardiac event.
D. Fatty degeneration is chronic atherosclerotic disease.
E. Caseous necrosis points towards tuberculosis.

resp-forensic.stem: Which sample is considered the most reliable and information-rich specimen for toxicological detection of strychnine during a forensic autopsy?
options: Gastric contents and unabsorbed seed fragments
why: A. Gastric contents frequently contain unabsorbed fragments or powder of nux-vomica seeds, making it the primary specimen for qualitative identification.
B. Expired air is used for volatile poisons like alcohol or cyanide.
C. CSF is useful for confirming drug distribution but is secondary to GI contents in solid ingestions.
D. Skin scrapings have no relevance to strychnine detection.
E. Fingernails are used for trace metals in long-term poisoning.

resp-forensic.stem: A patient presents with muscular rigidity and spasms following ingestion of an unknown toxin. You note that deep tendon reflexes are massively hyperactive and symmetric. Which mechanism explains this reflex hyperexcitability?
options: Depression of higher cortical inhibitory centres only
Blockade of inhibitory interneurones releasing glycine in the spinal cord
Excessive release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate
Direct stimulation of muscle fibre membrane voltage-gated channels
why: A. Strychnine acts primarily at the spinal cord level, not just by cortical depression.
B. Strychnine competitively blocks glycine receptors on postsynaptic motoneurones, removing spinal inhibition and producing exaggerated reflexes.
C. Acetylcholine excess causes fasciculations, not reflex spinal tetanic spasms.
D. Muscle membrane stimulation is secondary to spinal outflow, not a direct peripheral effect.
E. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of organophosphates.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the stability and post-mortem persistence of strychnine in body tissues is correct?
options: Strychnine is rapidly destroyed by putrefactive bacteria within 24 hours
Strychnine is extremely stable and can be detected in exhumed remains long after burial
Strychnine evaporates completely during the embalming process
Strychnine converts into harmless glucose within the stomach post-mortem
Strychnine binds permanently to bone matrix and cannot be extracted
why: A. Strychnine is notoriously resistant to putrefaction and persists in body tissues for months or years.
B. Its chemical stability makes it detectable in skeletal muscle, viscera, and bones even in advanced decomposition or exhumation cases.
C. It does not evaporate.
D. It does not convert into glucose.
E. While it can be extracted from viscera and muscle, it does not permanently bind to bone matrix beyond toxicological detection.

resp-forensic.stem: Which physical characteristic of nux-vomica seeds aids in their forensic identification when recovered from the stomach?
options: A smooth, shiny, bright red coat
A button-like shape with a central point and silky sheen from appressed hairs
A hollow tubular structure filled with milky latex
A wrinkled dark brown surface resembling a raisin
A hard woody capsule containing winged seeds
why: A. Nux-vomica seeds are not bright red.
B. They are characteristically disc-shaped, slightly concave-convex (button-like), with a central hilum and covered in silky, satiny hairs radiating from the centre.
C. Milky latex is characteristic of Papaver somniferum capsules.
D. Raisin-like appearance corresponds to dried fruits or certain seeds, not nux-vomica.
E. Winged seeds belong to different botanical families.

resp-forensic.stem: In cases of suspected strychnine homicide, what is the standard legal requirement under Pakistani criminal procedure regarding the preservation and dispatch of viscera?
options: Viscera must be washed in formalin before dispatch
Viscera must be preserved in saturated saline without formalin and sealed by the magistrate or police officer
Viscera should be frozen at minus twenty degrees Celsius without any preservative
Viscera are discarded after gross inspection
Viscera are preserved in absolute ethanol containing sulfuric acid
why: A. Formalin can interfere with certain toxicological analyses and is generally avoided when organic poisons are suspected; saturated saline is traditional.

B. Standard Pakistani forensic protocol requires viscera (stomach, piece of liver, intestine) to be preserved in saturated aqueous sodium chloride solution, sealed, and dispatched to the Chemical Examiner.
C. Freezing facilities are rarely available in rural transport chains.
D. Viscera are never discarded in suspicious deaths.
E. Ethanol is sometimes used, but saturated saline is the standard prescribed preservative.

resp-forensic.stem: Which clinical feature distinguishes strychnine poisoning from tetanus during the early stages of muscle stiffness?
options: Tetanus has a rapid onset within minutes, whereas strychnine takes days
Strychnine spasms begin abruptly and affect the limbs and trunk simultaneously with complete relaxation between spasms
Strychnine causes complete flaccid paralysis of the limbs
Tetanus is characterised by immediate loss of consciousness
why: A. Tetanus has an incubation period of days to weeks, whereas strychnine acts within 15 to 60 minutes.
B. Strychnine spasms are sudden, generalised, and intermittent with complete relaxation intervals initially, whereas tetanus has a gradual onset with persistent background rigidity.
C. Tetanus classically presents with early trismus (lockjaw).
D. Strychnine causes spasticity, not flaccid paralysis.
E. Consciousness is preserved in both tetanus and strychnine.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary cause of death in acute strychnine poisoning?
options: Asphyxia resulting from tetanic spasm of the respiratory muscles
why: A. Cerebral haemorrhage is not the primary mechanism of death.
B. Prolonged tetanic contraction of the intercostal muscles and diaphragm prevents ventilation, leading to fatal asphyxia.
C. Cardiac arrest is secondary to hypoxia, not primary arrhythmia.
D. Renal failure can occur secondary to rhabdomyolysis, but acute death is asphyxial.
E. Fulminant hepatic necrosis is typical of paracetamol or amanita poisoning.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following describes the taste of strychnine alkaloid when ingested?
options: Sour and acidic like lemon juice
why: A. Strychnine is not sweet.
B. Strychnine and its salts are renowned for their intense, persistent bitterness, detectable even at extreme dilutions.
C. It is not sour.
D. It is not salty or metallic.
E. While odorless, it is definitely not tasteless.

resp-forensic.stem: Which neurotransmitter receptor is the direct molecular target for strychnine antagonism in the mammalian spinal cord?
why: A. Nicotinic receptors are at the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia.
B. Strychnine is the classic competitive antagonist of inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord and brainstem.
C. GABA-A receptors are modulated by benzodiazepines, not blocked by strychnine.
D. NMDA receptors bind glutamate and are blocked by ketamine or PCP.
E. Mu-opioid receptors bind endorphins and opiates.

resp-forensic.stem: A patient presents with severe muscle spasms after ingesting a herbal remedy obtained from an unverified practitioner. The clinical picture includes clear consciousness, hyper-reflexia, and episodic arching of the back. Which forensic classification best fits strychnine in this context?
why: A. Corrosive poisons cause local tissue destruction (acids/alkalis).
B. Toxicological classification groups strychnine under neurotic spinal poisons because its primary site of action is the spinal cord.
C. Cardiac poisons include aconite and digitalis.
D. Somniferous poisons include opium and barbiturates.
E. Asphyxiants include carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide.

resp-forensic.stem: In a case of suspected strychnine poisoning, which auxiliary investigation performed on blood or urine during hospital admission is most definitive for confirmation?
options: High-performance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS)
why: A. Chromatographic techniques like HPLC-MS or GC-MS provide definitive qualitative and quantitative confirmation of strychnine.
B. Complete blood count is non-specific.
C. Electrolytes only guide supportive care.
D. Liver function tests assess hepatic injury, not poison presence.
E. Ketones indicate ketosis, not poisoning.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the typical lethal dose of pure strychnine in an untreated adult human?
why: A. The estimated fatal dose of strychnine in an adult is approximately 30 to 100 mg, making it extremely potent.
B. 10 to 20 grams is far above the lethal dose.
C. 500 to 800 mg is higher than the usual lethal threshold.
D. 1 to 2 kilograms is absurdly high.
E. Micrograms represent therapeutic ranges of potent drugs like digoxin, not strychnine.

resp-forensic.stem: During the examination of a body dead from strychnine poisoning, the medical examiner notes that the facial expression is fixed in a gruesome grin. What is the proper forensic term for this sign?
why: A. Opisthotonos is the backward arching of the spine.
B. Risus sardonicus is the characteristic facial spasm producing a sardonic grin, caused by contraction of facial muscles.
C. Emprosthotonos is the forward bending of the body.
D. Pleurothotonos is lateral bending of the body.
E. Trismus is jaw muscle spasm (lockjaw).

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following signs or symptoms is typically absent in pure strychnine poisoning, helping to differentiate it from anticholinergic or sympathomimetic toxicity?
options: Full preservation of consciousness throughout spasms
why: A. Consciousness is fully preserved in strychnine toxicity.

B. Visual hallucinations and prominent mydriasis are characteristic of anticholinergic or hallucinogenic poisoning, whereas strychnine preserves clear consciousness without prominent primary hallucinations.
C. Exaggerated startle reflex is a hallmark of strychnine action.
D. Intermittent tetanic spasms are characteristic.
E. Opisthotonos is characteristic.

resp-forensic.stem: If a victim survives the acute convulsive phase of strychnine poisoning for more than 24 hours, what is the clinical prognosis?
options: Death invariably occurs due to delayed multi-organ failure
Recovery is highly probable with appropriate supportive care and elimination of the poison
The patient develops permanent spastic quadriplegia
Delayed chronic neuropathy develops within weeks
Aplastic anaemia sets in due to bone marrow suppression
why: A. Survival past 24 hours generally indicates that the poison has been metabolised or excreted.
B. Strychnine is rapidly metabolised by hepatic microsomal enzymes; if the patient survives the initial asphyxial crisis, full recovery without permanent neurological sequelae is the rule.
C. Permanent spastic quadriplegia does not occur.
D. Chronic neuropathy is not a feature of strychnine.
E. Aplastic anaemia is associated with agents like benzene or chloramphenicol.

resp-forensic.stem: Which physiological mechanism explains why a minor tactile stimulus can trigger a massive convulsive seizure in a strychnine-poisoned patient?
options: Loss of postsynaptic recurrent inhibition mediated by Renshaw cells in the spinal cord
Direct mechanical stimulation of muscle spindles
Activation of cerebral pain centers by tactile cortex projections
why: A. Blood-brain barrier disruption is not the primary mechanism.
B. Strychnine blocks glycine receptors on motor neurones and Renshaw cells, abolishing spinal inhibitory feedback and causing sensory inputs to spread unchecked into massive motor output.
C. Muscle spindles are normal; the spinal processing is altered.
D. Tactile cortex projections do not cause titanic motor storms without spinal disinhibition.
E. Sympathetic blockade does not cause reflex spasms.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the recommended approach regarding emesis and gastric lavage in a patient presenting with active strychnine-induced convulsions?
options: Perform immediate aggressive gastric lavage without sedation
Emesis and lavage are absolutely contraindicated while convulsions are active, as the procedure can trigger fatal spasms
Administer high-dose syrup of ipecac immediately
Perform lavage only using warm tap water without airway protection
Force oral fluid intake to induce vomiting
why: A. Lavage without sedation during active convulsions is extremely dangerous.

B. Any physical manipulation or sensory stimulation during active convulsions can provoke lethal laryngospasm or extensor spasms; airway control and anticonvulsants must precede any GI decontamination.
C. Ipecac syrup is obsolete and unsafe in convulsing patients.
D. Lavage without airway protection risks aspiration and triggering spasms.
E. Forcing oral fluids risks aspiration.

resp-forensic.stem: Which legal term in Pakistani jurisprudence applies when someone administers strychnine with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, resulting in the victim's demise?
why: A. Qatl-i-Amd (intentional murder under the Pakistan Penal Code) applies when an act is done with the intention of causing death or bodily injury likely to cause death, such as administering a lethal poison.
B. Qatl-i-Shibh-i-Amd involves intent to cause harm with a weapon or means not normally lethal.
C. Qatl-bis-Sabab involves death caused by an unlawful act without direct intent.
D. Hurt applies to non-fatal injuries.
E. Sanha is a colloquial term, not a legal definition.

resp-forensic.stem: Which organ shows the highest concentration of strychnine during distribution studies following ingestion?
why: A. Strychnine is not heavily stored in adipose tissue due to its physicochemical properties.
B. While liver contains high amounts due to metabolism, skeletal muscle also contains significant amounts due to rapid blood perfusion and tissue binding.
C. Both liver and skeletal muscle accumulate high concentrations, making them primary viscera for toxicological analysis.
D. Tooth enamel does not absorb organic alkaloids.
E. Hair can incorporate trace poisons over time, but viscera and muscle are the primary quantitative organs.

resp-forensic.stem: In the differential diagnosis of spinal poisons, which plant extract is another notable spinal convulsant containing tetanising alkaloids (such as gelsemine or coniine analogues)?
why: A. Conium maculatum (poison hemlock) contains coniine, which causes ascending paralysis, though other plant toxins like gelsemium affect the spinal cord and nervous system.
B. Nicotiana tabacum contains nicotine (ganglionic stimulant).
C. Digitalis purpurea contains cardiac glycosides.
D. Ricinus communis contains ricin (toxalbumin).
E. Abrus precatorius contains abrin (toxalbumin).

resp-forensic.stem: During a forensic examination, you note that a body exhibits signs of cyanosis, petechiae in the conjunctivae, and dark fluid blood. The history mentions sudden tetanic spasms before death. Which conclusion is most justified?
options: Death was due to chronic wasting disease
Death was due to acute asphyxia, highly consistent with convulsant poisoning like strychnine
Death was due to acute myocardial infarction
Death was due to chronic renal failure
Death was due to diabetic coma
why: A. Chronic wasting disease does not cause rapid asphyxial signs.
B. Conjunctival petechiae, cyanosis, and dark fluid blood are classic triad findings of asphyxial death, which matches terminal tetanic fixation of respiration in strychnine poisoning.
C. Myocardial infarction lacks generalized tetanic spasm history.
D. Renal failure shows uraemic features.
E. Diabetic coma shows dehydration and fruity breath.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary route of elimination of absorbed strychnine from the human body?
options: Exhalation through the lungs as a volatile gas
Hepatic biotransformation followed by renal excretion of metabolites and unchanged drug
Secretion through sweat and sebaceous glands
why: A. Strychnine is not exhaled as a gas.
B. Strychnine is primarily metabolised by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and partly excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
C. Biliary excretion occurs, but renal excretion of metabolites is major.
D. Sweat excretion is negligible.
E. Bone deposition is not the primary elimination pathway.

resp-forensic.stem: Which clinical sign distinguishes strychnine poisoning from drug-induced dystonic reactions caused by neuroleptics?
options: Dystonia causes sustained oculogyric crises and torticollis without generalized painful extensor convulsions or preserved consciousness
Neuroleptics cause immediate fatal asphyxia via glycine receptor blockade
Strychnine causes deep coma with loss of reflexes
why: A. Neuroleptic dystonic reactions affect specific muscle groups (face, neck, eyes) and respond rapidly to anticholinergics, whereas strychnine causes generalized reflex extensor spasms and hyper-reflexia.
B. Strychnine causes spasticity, not flaccid paralysis.
C. Neuroleptics do not block glycine receptors.
D. Strychnine preserves consciousness and hyper-reflexia, not coma and absent reflexes.
E. Neuroleptics frequently cause muscle stiffness (dystonia/rigidity).

resp-forensic.stem: In cases of accidental ingestion of strychnine-containing rodenticides by children, what is the initial emergency priority before any diagnostic workup?
options: Securing the airway and ensuring a quiet, non-stimulating environment to prevent seizure induction
Administering oral emetics immediately in a brightly lit room
why: A. Airway management and sensory isolation are paramount to prevent fatal tetanic spasms triggered by examination or noise.
B. Bright lights and emetics can precipitate fatal seizures.
C. Lumbar puncture is unnecessary and dangerous in convulsing patients.
D. Total parenteral nutrition is for long-term support.
E. Psychiatric evaluation is irrelevant in emergency stabilisation.

resp-forensic.stem: Which pathological feature differentiates the rigor mortis of strychnine poisoning from heat rigor?
options: Heat rigor occurs due to coagulation of muscle proteins at high ambient temperatures, whereas strychnine rigor follows intense muscular exhaustion and ATP depletion with rapid onset
Heat rigor affects only the facial muscles
Strychnine rigor is permanent and never resolves
Heat rigor only occurs in poisoned individuals
why: A. Heat rigor is physical coagulation of muscle proteins from fire or high heat (above 65 degrees Celsius), whereas strychnine rigor is accelerated physiological rigor mortis due to profound ATP exhaustion from terminal convulsions.
B. Heat rigor affects all exposed muscle groups, causing pugilistic attitude.
C. Rigor mortis eventually resolves with putrefaction in both cases.
D. Heat rigor occurs in bodies exposed to extreme heat regardless of poison.
E. They have entirely different pathophysiological mechanisms.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary role of the Chemical Examiner in Pakistan when presented with viscera sealed by a magistrate in a suspected strychnine poisoning case?
options: To perform chemical and chromatographic tests to identify and quantify the poison and report findings to the court
To conduct the external post-mortem examination
To decide the quantum of punishment under Qisas and Diyat
why: A. Death certificates are issued by the attending doctor or police surgeon.
B. The Chemical Examiner analyses the submitted specimens using official toxicological protocols and issues an expert report for judicial proceedings.
C. Post-mortem examinations are performed by the medico-legal officer or professor of forensic medicine.
D. Police arrest perpetrators.
E. Courts determine punishment.

resp-forensic.stem: A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a sudden onset of violent convulsions. Witnesses report that his body arched backwards and his face was fixed in a rigid, horrific grin. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of action of the poison responsible for this condition?
options: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
Competitive antagonism of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Competitive antagonism of glycine receptors in the spinal cord
Irreversible blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels
Enhancement of GABA-A receptor chloride ion influx
why: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase causes cholinergic overstimulation, seen in organophosphate poisoning, not spinal rigidity.
Competitive antagonism of nicotinic receptors causes flaccid paralysis, typical of curare.
Competitive antagonism of glycine receptors in the spinal cord removes inhibitory control of motor neurons, leading to uninhibited reflex stimulation and characteristic tetanic convulsions.
Irreversible blockade of sodium channels arrests action potentials, causing local anaesthesia or paralysis.
Enhancement of GABA-A receptors causes central nervous system depression and relaxation, not tetanic spasms.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following classic botanical poisons acts primarily on the spinal cord to produce tetanic convulsions resembling tetanus?
why: Atropine is a belladonna alkaloid producing anticholinergic signs like delirium, dry mouth, and tachycardia.
Strychnos nux-vomica contains strychnine, the classic spinal poison causing violent tetanic spasms and opisthotonos.
Papaver somniferum yields opiates which cause central nervous system depression, respiratory depression, and miosis.
Aconitum napellus is a cardiac poison causing numbness, tingling, and fatal ventricular arrhythmias.
Digitalis purpurea is a cardiac glycoside causing bradycardia and lethal heart block or arrhythmias.

resp-forensic.stem: A young agricultural worker is found dead in a field with his body locked in extreme hyperextension, resting on his heels and occiput. Forensic examination confirms death due to asphyxia resulting from spasm of respiratory muscles. What is this classic posture known as?
why: Emprosthotonos is the forward bending of the body caused by muscle spasms, rare in strychnine poisoning.
Pleurothotonos is the lateral bending of the body due to unilateral muscle spasms.
Opisthotonos is the severe hyperextension and bridging of the body resting on the head and heels, classic for strychnine poisoning and tetanus.
Orthopnoea is shortness of breath relieved by sitting upright, common in cardiac or pulmonary failure.
Decerebrate rigidity is an extensor posture caused by brainstem lesions above the medulla, not spinal poisons.

resp-forensic.stem: During the autopsy of a victim who died from suspected strychnine poisoning, the forensic pathologist observes that the cadaver shows early and intense rigor mortis. What is the medico-legal significance of rigor mortis in strychnine poisoning?
options: It appears very late due to profound muscle exhaustion
It is completely absent due to depletion of muscle glycogen
It sets in rapidly and intensely due to violent premortem muscular activity
It affects only the lower limbs, sparing the respiratory muscles
It is indistinguishable from cadaveric spasm and prevents estimation of time since death
why: It does not appear late; intense premortem activity accelerates ATP depletion.
It is not absent; rather, it is intensified by the severe muscular contractions.
It sets in rapidly and intensely because the violent tetanic convulsions consume all muscle ATP prematurely, locking the fibres.
It affects the entire skeletal musculature, especially the trunk and limbs.
While rapid, it is distinct from true cadaveric spasm and follows normal post-mortem cooling and progression.

resp-forensic.stem: A forensic toxicologist is performing a chemical analysis on stomach contents from a poisoning case. The tests yield a bright red colour when treated with concentrated sulphuric acid and potassium dichromate crystals. Which alkaloid is being identified?
why: Morphine gives a purple to violet colour with Marquis reagent or nitric acid.
Atropine gives the Vitali-Morin test producing a violet colour turning red-brown with alcoholic potash.
Strychnine produces a characteristic play of colours (deep blue passing to purple, crimson, and finally orange-yellow) when oxidised with sulphuric acid and potassium dichromate.
Barbiturates are identified by the Zwikker test producing a violet-blue complex.
Arsenic is detected by the Marsh test or Reinsch test, not colour tests with dichromate and acid.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary site of action within the central nervous system for strychnine?
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
why: The cerebral cortex is not the primary site where strychnine acts to produce motor spasms.
Basal ganglia are involved in extrapyramidal disorders, not primary strychnine toxicity.
Strychnine acts predominantly on the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord by blocking post-synaptic inhibition.
Medullary centres are affected secondarily via hypoxia during prolonged spasms, not as the primary site.
Cerebellar cells are spared from the direct convulsant action of strychnine.

resp-forensic.stem: A differential diagnosis must be made between tetanus and strychnine poisoning in a patient presenting with generalized muscle spasms. Which of the following clinical features strongly favours strychnine poisoning over tetanus?
options: Presence of a clear history of a puncture wound or laceration
Trismus (lockjaw) appearing as the very first and most prominent sign
Complete relaxation of muscles between convulsive episodes
A prolonged incubation period lasting between 7 to 14 days
Gradual onset of stiffness starting in the neck and jaw
why: A puncture wound points towards Clostridium tetani infection, not strychnine ingestion.
Trismus is an early and prominent feature of tetanus, whereas in strychnine poisoning, the jaw muscles are often affected last.
In strychnine poisoning, muscles relax completely between spasms triggered by external stimuli, unlike tetanus where baseline rigidity persists.
Tetanus has an incubation period of days to weeks, whereas strychnine symptoms start within minutes to an hour.
Gradual onset of stiffness is characteristic of tetanus, while strychnine causes sudden, explosive onset.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters is competitively antagonised at its post-synaptic receptor by strychnine?
why: Acetylcholine acts at neuromuscular junctions and autonomic ganglia, blocked by curare or atropine.
GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, blocked by picrotoxin or bicuculline.
Glycine is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord, and strychnine is its specific competitive antagonist.
Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter, blocked by agents like ketamine.
Dopamine is a catecholamine involved in movement and reward pathways.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the immediate cause of death in a fatal case of strychnine poisoning if left untreated?
options: Irreversible cerebral haemorrhage due to high blood pressure
Asphyxia secondary to tetanic spasm of the respiratory muscles
Severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance from vomiting
Uncontrolled hyperthermia leading to multi-organ failure
Massive gastrointestinal haemorrhage from gastric ulcers
why: Cerebral haemorrhage is not the primary mechanism of death in strychnine toxicity.
Asphyxia due to sustained spasm of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles prevents pulmonary ventilation, causing rapid death.
Vomiting is not a prominent feature of strychnine poisoning.
Hyperthermia can occur due to muscle activity, but asphyxia is the immediate fatal mechanism.
Gastrointestinal bleeding is not caused by strychnine.

resp-forensic.stem: Management of a patient with acute strychnine poisoning requires urgent medical intervention. Which of the following therapeutic measures is contraindicated or hazardous during the acute convulsive phase?
options: Administration of intravenous diazepam to control convulsions
Ensuring absolute quiet and dimming lights to prevent sensory triggers
Attempting forceful gastric lavage immediately without airway protection
Providing mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen
Administering active charcoal via a nasogastric tube if the airway is secured
why: Intravenous diazepam enhances GABA transmission and is essential for stopping muscle spasms.
Minimising sensory stimuli is crucial because noise, touch, or light trigger violent reflex spasms.
Attempting forceful gastric lavage in an unparalysed, conscious patient triggers severe, fatal reflex convulsions; it is hazardous without prior airway control and sedation.
Mechanical ventilation is life-saving when respiratory muscle spasms cause asphyxia.
Activated charcoal adsorbs residual poison in the stomach if the patient is adequately sedated or protected.

resp-forensic.stem: A twenty-year-old female is brought to the accident and emergency department after intentionally ingesting thirty tablets of an over-the-counter analgesic in a suicide attempt. She is currently asymptomatic, but serum drug levels drawn four hours post-ingestion confirm a severe toxic overdose. Which of the following specific antidotes must be administered immediately within eight hours to prevent irreversible hepatic necrosis?
why: Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist used for benzodiazepine reversal, not paracetamol.
Naloxone is the specific opioid receptor antagonist used for opioid-induced respiratory depression.
N-acetylcysteine acts as a glutathione precursor, neutralising the toxic NAPQI metabolite of paracetamol and preventing centrilobular hepatic necrosis when given early.
Atropine is an anticholinergic drug used in organophosphate and carbamate poisonings.
Deferoxamine is a specific iron-chelating agent used for acute iron poisoning.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following pathological mechanisms best explains the development of centrilobular hepatic necrosis following a massive paracetamol overdose?
options: Direct depletion of hepatic glycogen stores leading to cellular starvation
Formation of toxic NAPQI via cytochrome P450 which binds to cellular macromolecules
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in the inner mitochondrial membrane
Inhibition of hepatic aldehyde dehydrogenase causing toxic acetaldehyde accumulation
Competitive blockade of vitamin K epoxide reductase preventing clotting factor synthesis
why: Glycogen depletion is a secondary metabolic feature, not the primary mechanism of necrosis.
Paracetamol is metabolised by CYP450 into N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine, which depletes glutathione and covalently binds to vital cellular proteins.
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation is the classic mechanism of salicylate toxicity.
Inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase is the mechanism of action of disulfiram.
Competitive blockade of vitamin K epoxide reductase is the mechanism of action of warfarin.

resp-forensic.stem: A thirty-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with severe metabolic acidosis, tinnitus, hyperventilation, and confusion. Laboratory investigations reveal a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Which of the following therapeutic agents is primarily responsible for this clinical presentation?
why: Paracetamol toxicity causes hepatotoxicity and elevated liver enzymes, but not primary tinnitus or early hyperventilation.
Aspirin uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, stimulating the respiratory centre directly and causing a mixed acid-base disturbance along with tinnitus.
Morphine overdose causes central nervous system depression, miosis, and bradypnoea.
Digoxin toxicity causes visual disturbances, hyperkalaemia, and various cardiac arrhythmias.
Diazepam overdose causes central nervous system depression with minimal respiratory depression unless combined with alcohol.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following clinical features is classically observed in chronic salicylate poisoning, also known as salicylism, distinguishing it from acute overdose?
options: Prominent gastrointestinal bleeding and severe vomiting
Severe neurotoxicity including confusion, hallucinations, and lethargy
Rapid development of fulminant hepatic failure within twenty-four hours
Marked hypotension refractory to intravenous fluid resuscitation
Immediate onset of non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
why: Gastrointestinal symptoms are common to both acute and chronic overdoses.

Chronic salicylate poisoning often presents subtly with central nervous system manifestations like confusion, hallucinations, and lethargy, which can be misdiagnosed as encephalopathy or psychiatric illness.
Fulminant hepatic failure is characteristic of paracetamol poisoning, not salicylates.
Refractory hypotension is a feature of severe beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity.
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema occurs in severe acute overdoses, particularly in older adults.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of naloxone when administered to reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression?
options: Agonist at mu-opioid receptors to stimulate respiratory drive
Competitive antagonist at mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors
Non-competitive inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase at respiratory junctions
Direct smooth muscle relaxant acting on bronchial smooth muscle fibres
Potent GABA-A receptor antagonist stimulating central arousal pathways
why: Naloxone is an antagonist, not an agonist.
Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist with high affinity for mu receptors, rapidly displacing agonists and reversing respiratory depression.
It has no anticholinesterase activity.
It does not act as a direct bronchial smooth muscle relaxant.
It is not a GABA-A antagonist; flumazenil is used for GABA-A receptor reversal.

resp-forensic.stem: A four-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after swallowing several colourful iron tablets prescribed for his mother's antenatal care. He presents with severe vomiting, haematemesis, and abdominal pain. Which of the following pathological stages is expected to occur twelve to twenty-four hours post-ingestion if he survives the initial gastrointestinal phase?
options: Complete clinical recovery and normalisation of all serum parameters
A latent period of relative clinical quiescence and apparent stabilisation
Onset of fulminant hepatic failure with profound hypoglycaemia
Development of irreversible renal cortical necrosis and anuria
Immediate progression to circulatory collapse and metabolic acidosis
why: Complete recovery does not occur spontaneously without chelation therapy after a toxic dose.

Acute iron poisoning classically progresses in stages: GI irritation (0 to 6 hours), relative quiescence/latent period (6 to 24 hours), shock and metabolic acidosis (12 to 72 hours), and hepatic injury followed later by gastrointestinal scarring.
Hepatic injury occurs later, typically in stage four (2 to 5 days).
Renal failure can occur during shock, but the 12 to 24 hour mark is classically known as the latent stabilisation phase before systemic toxicity hits.
Circulatory collapse typically occurs in stage three, following the latent period.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following specific laboratory investigations is most crucial for guiding the initial management and determining the need for antidotal therapy in acute paracetamol poisoning?
options: Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen
Serum paracetamol concentration plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram
Serum salicylate level and arterial blood gases
Serum iron level and total iron-binding capacity
Serum electrolyte panel and plasma osmolal gap
why: Renal parameters assess secondary organ involvement but do not guide early antidotal treatment.
The Rumack-Matthew nomogram correlates timed serum paracetamol concentrations (drawn between 4 and 24 hours post-ingestion) with the risk of hepatotoxicity to guide N-acetylcysteine therapy.
Salicylate levels and blood gases are used for aspirin toxicity.
Iron levels and TIBC are used for acute iron poisoning assessments.
Osmolal gap is used for toxic alcohol ingestions such as methanol or ethylene glycol.

resp-forensic.stem: A patient with severe barbiturate overdose presents in a deep coma with hypotension, hypothermia, and absent reflexes. Which of the following is the mainstay of modern management for this condition?
options: Administration of specific physiological stimulants such as bemegride
Aggressive forced alkaline diuresis to enhance renal elimination
Supportive intensive care, airway maintenance, and prevention of complications
Immediate surgical haemoperfusion combined with peritoneal dialysis
Administration of flumazenil to reverse central nervous system depression
why: Central nervous system stimulants are obsolete and dangerous as they induce convulsions without improving survival.
Forced diuresis is no longer recommended due to the high risk of pulmonary and cerebral oedema.
Supportive care (airway, breathing, circulation, prevention of aspiration and pressure sores) remains the cornerstone of barbiturate poisoning management.
Extracorporeal removal is rarely required unless toxicity is life-threatening and unresponsive to supportive care.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not barbiturates.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following features is a classic toxicological finding in acute tricyclic antidepressant poisoning resulting from blockade of fast sodium channels in the myocardium?
options: Shortened PR interval and tall peaked T waves on the electrocardiogram
Prolonged QRS complex duration and right axis deviation of the terminal 40 milliseconds
Marked sinus bradycardia unresponsive to intravenous atropine
Complete atrioventricular dissociation with ventricular escape rhythms
Prominent U waves with severe resting hypokalaemia
why: Shortened PR interval is seen in conditions like hypercalcaemia or pre-excitation syndromes.

Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac fast sodium channels, causing QRS prolongation (greater than 100 milliseconds) and a terminal rightward axis shift (terminal 40-ms vector directed rightward towards an upright R wave in aVR).
Tricyclics typically cause sinus tachycardia due to their anticholinergic properties.
Advanced heart block can occur, but QRS widening is the hallmark sign.
Prominent U waves are classic for hypokalaemia or quinidine toxicity.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which deferoxamine exerts its therapeutic effect in acute iron poisoning?
options: Precipitating ionic iron in the gastric lumen to form insoluble complexes
Chelating trivalent ferric iron to form a water-soluble complex excreted in urine
Competitive inhibition of mucosal iron transport proteins in the duodenum
Blocking the intracellular incorporation of iron into protoporphyrin IX
Increasing hepatic synthesis of ferritin to sequester excess circulating iron
why: Precipitation in the gut is achieved by agents like sodium bicarbonate, not deferoxamine.

Deferoxamine is a specific chelating agent that binds circulating and tissue ferric (Fe3+) iron, forming ferrioxamine, which is renally excreted and imparts a characteristic vin-rosé (pinkish-red) colour to the urine.
It does not act by blocking mucosal transport in the gastrointestinal lumen directly.
It does not interfere with protoporphyrin IX incorporation.
It directly chelates free iron rather than stimulating endogenous ferritin storage.

resp-forensic.stem: A 30-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency department after ingesting a grey tablet used for grain storage. His breath smells of decaying fish. What is the toxic gas responsible for his symptoms?
why: Incorrect; CO has no characteristic fishy smell.
Correct; aluminium phosphide releases phosphine gas ($PH_3$), smelling of decaying fish or garlic.
Incorrect; cyanide smells of bitter almonds.
Incorrect; hydrogen sulphide smells of rotten eggs.
Incorrect; ammonia has a sharp, pungent odour.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following cellular enzymes is primarily inhibited by aluminium phosphide?
why: Incorrect; inhibited by organophosphates and carbamates.
Correct; phosphine inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, halting mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
Incorrect; inhibited by MAO inhibitors.
Incorrect; inhibited by lead.
Incorrect; inhibited by cardiac glycosides.

resp-forensic.stem: Why is plain water strictly avoided for early gastric lavage in a patient who has just ingested aluminium phosphide?
options: Water accelerates the hydrolysis and release of phosphine gas
why: Incorrect; perforation is a late risk from corrosion, but not the reason water is withheld.
Correct; moisture speeds up the chemical reaction generating toxic phosphine gas.
Incorrect; there is no specific antidote.
Incorrect; water does not cause hypernatremia.
Incorrect; seizures are not the primary reason.

resp-forensic.stem: Which solution is traditionally recommended for gastric lavage in aluminium phosphide poisoning to detoxify unabsorbed poison?
why: Incorrect; saline does not oxidise phosphine.
Incorrect; sodium bicarbonate corrects acidosis but does not oxidise the poison.
Correct; potassium permanganate ($1:10,000$) oxidises phosphine into non-toxic phosphates.
Incorrect; hydrogen peroxide is too caustic.
Incorrect; magnesium sulphate is a cathartic, not an oxidiser.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the hallmark cardiovascular feature of acute aluminium phosphide toxicity?
why: Incorrect; tachyarrhythmias may occur, but profound shock is the hallmark.
Correct; direct myocardial depression leads to profound, treatment-resistant shock.
Incorrect; aluminium phosphide causes hypotension, not hypertension.
Incorrect; bradycardia is not the primary presentation.
Incorrect; right ventricular hypertrophy is chronic.

resp-forensic.stem: A patient survives the first 48 hours of severe aluminium phosphide poisoning. Which delayed organ complications must clinicians monitor for?
options: Acute hepatic necrosis and acute renal failure
Chronic peptic ulcer disease and pyloric stenosis
why: Incorrect; pulmonary fibrosis is characteristic of paraquat.
Correct; survivors frequently develop secondary liver and kidney failure.
Incorrect; bone marrow failure is not a feature.
Incorrect; neuropathy is seen in heavy metal poisoning.
Incorrect; strictures are rare.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary commercial use and nature of paraquat?
why: Incorrect; paraquat is a herbicide, not an insecticide.
Correct; paraquat is a potent, non-selective contact herbicide.
Incorrect; it is not used as a rodenticide.
Incorrect; it is not a fungicide.
Incorrect; aluminium phosphide is a fumigant.

resp-forensic.stem: Which biochemical mechanism underlies paraquat-induced tissue damage?
options: Redox cycling and generation of superoxide radicals
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation via protonophoric action
why: Incorrect; mechanism of organophosphates.
Correct; paraquat undergoes redox cycling to form destructive reactive oxygen species.
Incorrect; mechanism of alkylating agents.
Incorrect; mechanism of dinitrophenols.
Incorrect; mechanism of fluoride.

resp-forensic.stem: Which organ system bears the brunt of long-term fatal injury in paraquat poisoning?
why: Incorrect; CNS is minimally affected compared to lungs.
Incorrect; cardiovascular collapse is the hallmark of aluminium phosphide, not paraquat.
Correct; active uptake into the lungs leads to fatal alveolar damage and fibrosis.
Incorrect; GI damage is acute and caustic, but not the cause of delayed death.
Incorrect; bone marrow is not the primary target.

resp-forensic.stem: Why is high-flow oxygen therapy strictly contraindicated in early paraquat poisoning?
options: It supercharges redox cycling and accelerates free radical lung destruction
It causes severe acute respiratory alkalosis
why: Incorrect; laryngeal spasm is not caused by oxygen.
Correct; supplemental oxygen provides the substrate for superoxide generation, worsening lung injury.
Incorrect; oxygen does not interact with Fuller's earth.
Incorrect; it does not cause respiratory alkalosis.
Incorrect; it does not cause encephalopathy.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the role of Fuller's earth or activated charcoal when administered urgently after paraquat ingestion?
options: As a systemic antidote neutralising circulating paraquat
As a gastrointestinal adsorbent to prevent absorption
As a potent osmotic laxative to speed elimination
As a demulcent coating the oesophagus
why: Incorrect; neither acts as a systemic antidote.
Correct; adsorbents bind paraquat in the gut lumen, preventing systemic absorption.
Incorrect; while charcoal is given with cathartics, its primary role is adsorption.
Incorrect; it does not stimulate respiration.
Incorrect; demulcents soothe, but Fuller's earth adsorbs.

resp-forensic.stem: Which bedside qualitative test can detect paraquat in the urine of an acutely poisoned patient?
why: Incorrect; Prussian blue test is for iron or cyanide depending on context.
Correct; sodium dithionite in sodium hydroxide turns blue-green in the presence of paraquat.
Incorrect; Marquis test is for opiates and amphetamines.
Incorrect; barium chloride tests for sulphates.
Incorrect; Gunning's test is for acetone.

resp-forensic.stem: What physical sign in the oral cavity is virtually diagnostic of acute liquid paraquat ingestion?
options: Bluish-black discoloration of the gums (Burton's line)
Caustic burns and greenish staining of the oral mucosa
why: Incorrect; Burton's line is characteristic of chronic lead poisoning.
Correct; corrosive local action causes burns and stains from the dye in commercial paraquat.
Incorrect; seen in scarlet fever or Kawasaki disease.
Incorrect; seen in candidiasis or diphtheria.
Incorrect; seen in heavy metal poisoning or cholinergic excess.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the ultimate cause of death in fatal paraquat cases that survive the initial corrosive GI phase?
why: Incorrect; GI bleeding is rarely fatal on its own.
Incorrect; cardiac arrest is typical of aluminium phosphide.
Correct; irreversible alveolar destruction and fibrosis lead to fatal asphyxia.
Incorrect; liver failure occurs but is secondary to pulmonary death.
Incorrect; renal failure is common, but lungs fail first.

resp-forensic.stem: Compare the post-mortem appearance of the stomach in aluminium phosphide versus paraquat poisoning. Which feature distinguishes paraquat?
options: Severe corrosive ulceration with greenish staining
Greyish-black congestion with a garlic odour
Perforated anterior gastric wall with gas bubbles
why: Incorrect; mucosa is ulcerated, not absent.
Correct; paraquat causes severe corrosive gastritis and often retains the green/blue dye staining.
Incorrect; greyish-black congestion and garlic odour belong to aluminium phosphide.
Incorrect; yellow mucosa is seen in nitric acid or picric acid poisoning.
Incorrect; gas bubbles in tissue are seen in gas gangrene.

resp-forensic.stem: A medical student asks why aluminium phosphide is so lethal. Which physiological system fails first and most catastrophically?
why: Incorrect; CNS depression occurs late.
Correct; cardiovascular collapse and refractory hypotension occur within hours.
Incorrect; renal failure is delayed.
Incorrect; pulmonary edema occurs, but cardiovascular collapse dominates early.
Incorrect; GI symptoms occur first, but are not the immediate cause of death.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following interventions has proven effective in improving survival rates in severe aluminium phosphide poisoning?
options: Magnesium sulphate infusion and aggressive supportive care
why: Incorrect; atropine/pralidoxime is for organophosphates, though atropine is sometimes used for phosphine-induced bradycardia.
Correct; magnesium sulphate improves cardiac membrane stability, combined with supportive care.
Incorrect; penicillamine is for copper/lead.
Incorrect; hyperbaric oxygen is ineffective and hazardous.
Incorrect; NAC is for paracetamol.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary legal and public health concern regarding aluminium phosphide and paraquat in Pakistan?
options: Accidental industrial emission in urban centers
Widespread availability leading to high rates of intentional self-poisoning
why: Incorrect; these are agricultural agents, not urban industrial emissions.
Correct; easy access in rural areas makes them leading agents for impulsive suicide.
Incorrect; contamination of municipal water is rare.
Incorrect; not related to textiles.
Incorrect; they are not precursors for narcotics.

resp-forensic.stem: A patient presents with acute paraquat poisoning. Haemodialysis and haemoperfusion are sometimes attempted. What is their primary purpose?
options: To remove circulating paraquat from the bloodstream early after ingestion
why: Correct; haemoperfusion (especially charcoal haemoperfusion) can remove circulating herbicide if performed very early.
Incorrect; dialysis corrects electrolytes, but paraquat clearance is the main goal.
Incorrect; dialysis cannot reverse established pulmonary fibrosis.
Incorrect; does not reverse liver necrosis.
Incorrect; perforation requires surgery.

resp-forensic.stem: Which poison produces phosphine gas upon contact with gastric acid or water?
why: Correct; zinc phosphide, like aluminium phosphide, releases phosphine gas upon contact with moisture/acid.
Incorrect; organophosphates do not release phosphine.
Incorrect; carbamates do not release phosphine.
Incorrect; cyanide releases hydrogen cyanide gas.
Incorrect; strychnine is an alkaloid.

resp-forensic.stem: An agricultural worker ingests a mouthful of paraquat. He is asymptomatic on presentation. What should be the attending doctor's approach?
options: Admit him for observation, decontamination, and supportive care
why: Incorrect; paraquat toxicity is notoriously insidious and often fatal even after trivial ingestion.
Correct; hospital admission, decontamination, and close monitoring are mandatory for all ingestions.
Incorrect; pneumonectomy is not indicated.
Incorrect; oxygen is contraindicated.
Incorrect; discharge is extremely dangerous.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the typical appearance of aluminium phosphide tablets prior to use?
options: Clear colourless liquid in amber bottles
Dark grey or dark brown tablets with a pungent smell
Bright green granules in paper packets
why: Incorrect; liquid formulation describes paraquat.
Correct; aluminium phosphide tablets are typically dark grey or greenish-grey and release phosphine on exposure to air.
Incorrect; green granules describe paraquat or certain baits.
Incorrect; white powder does not describe wheat pills.
Incorrect; red paste does not describe it.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following findings is characteristically absent in acute aluminium phosphide poisoning?
why: Incorrect; metabolic acidosis is prominent due to cellular hypoxia and shock.
Incorrect; refractory hypotension is a hallmark.
Incorrect; fishy/garlic breath odour is characteristic.
Correct; miosis and excessive secretions are features of organophosphate poisoning, not aluminium phosphide.
Incorrect; myocardial depression is a primary feature.

resp-forensic.stem: In a post-mortem examination of a victim who died from paraquat poisoning, which histological finding is expected in the lungs if survival exceeded one week?
options: Caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells
Intense alveolar inflammation followed by widespread intra-alveolar and interstitial fibrosis
Hyaline membrane disease typical of neonates
Centrilobular emphysema and goblet cell hyperplasia
why: Incorrect; granulomas suggest tuberculosis or fungal infection.
Incorrect; abscesses suggest bacterial bronchopneumonia.
Correct; classic pathology shows early exudative alveolitis progressing to relentless pulmonary fibrosis.
Incorrect; neonatal hyaline membrane disease is surfactant deficiency.
Incorrect; emphysema is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

resp-forensic.stem: Which management step is critical in the immediate decontamination phase of oral paraquat ingestion?
options: Immediate administration of potassium permanganate lavage
Immediate administration of Fuller's earth or activated charcoal
High-flow oxygen administration to prevent hypoxia
Immediate gastric lavage with copious plain water
Intravenous infusion of sodium bicarbonate and glucose
why: Incorrect; potassium permanganate is for aluminium phosphide.
Correct; Fuller's earth or activated charcoal adsorbs paraquat in the gut and limits absorption.
Incorrect; oxygen is contraindicated.
Incorrect; copious water is dangerous in aluminium phosphide, and corrosive risk applies in paraquat.
Incorrect; bicarbonate corrects acidosis but decontamination comes first.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary reason why mortality remains exceptionally high in established aluminium phosphide poisoning?
options: Lack of awareness of the ingestion
Rapid absorption and irreversible inhibition of mitochondrial respiration leading to shock
Delayed onset of symptoms exceeding 7 days
why: Incorrect; history of ingestion is usually clear.
Correct; rapid absorption of phosphine gas causes swift, irreversible cellular energy failure and refractory shock.
Incorrect; symptoms start within minutes.
Incorrect; bronchospasm is not the main lethal mechanism.
Incorrect; seizures are rare.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following features distinguishes paraquat poisoning from organophosphate poisoning?
options: Delayed pulmonary fibrosis leading to asphyxia
why: Incorrect; fasciculations occur in organophosphates.
Correct; pulmonary fibrosis is hallmark for paraquat, absent in organophosphates.
Incorrect; bronchial secretions are cholinergic features.
Incorrect; organophosphates cause cholinergic crisis.
Incorrect; garlic breath odour is found in aluminium phosphide or organophosphates (some formulations).

resp-forensic.stem: A patient presents with acute aluminium phosphide poisoning. Laboratory investigations show severe metabolic acidosis. What is the main contributor to this acidosis?
options: Lactic acidosis secondary to cellular hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism
Renal tubular acidosis from direct nephrotoxicity
Hyperchloremic acidosis from normal saline infusion
why: Correct; mitochondrial failure halts oxidative phosphorylation, forcing anaerobic metabolism and massive lactic acid production.
Incorrect; renal failure contributes later, but early acidosis is lactic.
Incorrect; ketoacidosis is not primary.
Incorrect; acidosis is metabolic, not respiratory.
Incorrect; saline is not the primary cause.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the legal status of aluminium phosphide in Pakistan regarding its sale and distribution?
options: Completely banned for all purposes under federal law
Regulated agricultural pesticide available through licensed dealers
Freely available over-the-counter in grocery stores without restriction
Classified as a scheduled narcotic under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act
Available only in hospital pharmacies on prescription
why: Incorrect; it is not completely banned as it is vital for grain storage.
Correct; legally a restricted agricultural pesticide, though enforcement of licensing is frequently lax.
Incorrect; by law it requires licensing, though illegal OTC sales occur.
Incorrect; it is a pesticide, not a narcotic.
Incorrect; not sold in hospital pharmacies.

resp-forensic.stem: In paraquat poisoning, what is the significance of the sodium dithionite urine test?
options: It provides a quantitative measurement of blood paraquat levels
It provides a rapid qualitative confirmation of paraquat ingestion
It determines the degree of pulmonary fibrosis
It tests for concomitant organophosphate ingestion
why: Incorrect; it is qualitative, not quantitative.
Correct; a positive test (blue/green colour) confirms presence of paraquat in urine.
Incorrect; it does not measure fibrosis.
Incorrect; it does not measure liver function.
Incorrect; it is specific for paraquat/diquat.

resp-forensic.stem: Which of the following signs or symptoms is typically seen in the acute phase of paraquat poisoning?
options: Severe corrosive ulceration of the upper gastrointestinal tract
why: Correct; paraquat is a strong corrosive, causing severe burns to the mouth, throat, and stomach.
Incorrect; miosis and paralysis are seen in organophosphates.
Incorrect; cherry-red skin is carbon monoxide poisoning.
Incorrect; extrapyramidal signs are seen in neuroleptics or manganese.
Incorrect; bradycardia/salivation are cholinergic.

resp-forensic.stem: Why are antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase or N-acetylcysteine of limited clinical efficacy in established paraquat poisoning?
options: They cannot cross the blood-brain barrier
The rate of free radical generation vastly overwhelms endogenous and exogenous antioxidant capacity
They accelerate renal excretion of paraquat
They neutralize the bittering agent in paraquat
why: Incorrect; antioxidants do not destroy mucosa.
Incorrect; brain penetration is not the limiting factor for lung toxicity.
Correct; redox cycling produces reactive oxygen species at a rate that overwhelms antioxidant defenses.
Incorrect; they do not increase renal excretion.
Incorrect; bittering agent is irrelevant to antioxidant efficacy.

resp-forensic.stem: Which poison is associated with the release of phosphine gas and carries a mortality rate exceeding 70-80% in developing countries?
why: Incorrect; paraquat mortality is also high, but aluminium phosphide is classically cited for its exceptionally high rapid mortality from shock.
Correct; aluminium phosphide has a notoriously high mortality rate due to refractory shock.
Incorrect; malathion is an organophosphate with lower case fatality.
Incorrect; strychnine causes tetanic convulsions.
Incorrect; zinc phosphide is also toxic, but aluminium phosphide is the wheat pill of primary concern.

resp-forensic.stem: A patient presents 6 hours after ingesting paraquat. He is vomiting and has oral burns. Which diagnostic imaging should be ordered to assess early thoracic involvement?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
why: Correct; chest X-ray establishes baseline lung fields and monitors for subsequent alveolitis and pulmonary edema.
Incorrect; MRI brain is not indicated for paraquat.
Incorrect; ultrasound abdomen assesses liver/kidneys but not lungs.
Incorrect; echocardiogram evaluates heart, which is not the primary paraquat target.
Incorrect; barium swallow evaluates oesophageal strictures late, not early lung injury.

resp-forensic.stem: What is the primary mechanism by which magnesium sulphate is thought to benefit patients with aluminium phosphide poisoning?
options: Membrane stabilisation and anti-arrhythmic effects countering phosphine toxicity
Competitive antagonism at the acetylcholine receptor
why: Incorrect; it is not a chelating agent for aluminium.
Correct; magnesium restores intracellular magnesium depleted by phosphine, stabilizing myocardial membranes and reducing arrhythmias.
Incorrect; it does not neutralise gastric acid.
Incorrect; it is not an anticholinergic.
Incorrect; it acts as a cathartic, not an emetic.
